items.title: [MIT Technology Review] The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
items.content_html: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects…

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
items.content_html: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

items.title: [phys.org] Neolithic tomb pots point to fermented milk offerings in Denmark
items.content_html: Researchers studying 330 Neolithic pots from western Zealand, Denmark, found corrosion on 31; 29 came from passage tombs. In experiments with reconstructed vessels, fresh, unpasteurized milk produced damage resembling the marks on ancient pottery, while beer and mead did not. The findings, published in Antiquity, suggest fermented dairy may have been placed with the dead, although corrosion alone cannot identify the contents with certainty. The results challenge an earlier interpretation that the corroded pots held beer, an idea based partly on evidence from brewing communities elsewhere. Fermentation makes milk more acidic, and the researchers say fermented dairy products could also have been easier to digest and lasted longer. Lead author Lone Claudi-Hansen, an archaeologist, said she hopes to examine pottery from other parts of Denmark to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere.

items.title: [universetoday.com] Lunar craters could shield habitats from reactor radiation
items.content_html: Researchers studying a proposed lunar nuclear power system say crater walls and other natural terrain could block reactor radiation from reaching a future base, reducing the need to transport heavy shielding from Earth. NASA’s planned 40-kilowatt reactor faces a design constraint: the full system must weigh less than 6,000 kilograms for transport by rover. The findings are based on computer simulations, not a physical test. The researchers also warn that the area around an operating reactor would remain dangerous, and reflected neutrons could require a no-fly zone over the site.

items.title: [livescience.com] Four Guangxi fossil teeth point to Denisovans and another ancient lineage
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers analyzing four fossil teeth from two caves in China’s Guangxi region identified Denisovan-related remains and evidence of a potentially distinct ancient human lineage, according to a study published in Nature on Nov. 25. The two Longchuandong teeth align with Denisovans, while two teeth from Chuanshandong—at least 100,800 years old—have traits that do not readily match any known East Asian Homo group. The findings suggest different archaic human populations lived in southern China during overlapping periods, but researchers cannot yet confidently assign the Chuanshandong teeth to a named group. Warm, humid conditions in the region hinder ancient DNA preservation, so researchers analyzed tooth shape and proteins. They say more fossils and molecular evidence are needed to establish the teeth’s evolutionary relationships.

items.title: [science.org] Stanford researchers find nanoscale niobium phosphide wires outperform copper
items.content_html: Stanford University researchers reported that ultrathin niobium phosphide ribbons conduct electricity more efficiently than copper wires of comparable size, with resistivity falling as the ribbons narrow. The study, published in Nature, tested ribbons as small as 5–6 nanometers wide and about 1.5 nanometers thick. Resistance in the tiny connections linking transistors can delay signals in advanced chips. Researchers disagree about whether the material’s topological properties explain the drop in resistivity. Outside scientists questioned whether a niobium surface layer influenced the measurements, and Stanford physicist and study leader Eric Pop acknowledged that other explanations remain possible.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
items.content_html: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
items.content_html: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

items.title: [hackaday.com] Researchers model helium bubbles to limit metal buildup in molten-salt reactors
items.content_html: Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute used computer simulations to study how replenishing helium bubbles could prevent radioactive metal particles from accumulating in molten-salt reactor systems. The particles can coat heat exchangers, trapping heat and reducing reactor efficiency; the models indicate that adding fresh bubbles can sustain the bubbles’ ability to collect the metals. The team combined experimental data from the 1960s and 1970s with Argonne’s SAM reactor-safety software to track tellurium-132 under different bubble-flow conditions. The study was published in the journal Nuclear Technology. Its findings are based on simulations, not experimental validation of the proposed operating approach.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Tiny solar tracker records hummingbird’s 4,055-mile migration to Alaska
items.content_html:
🪶 🌲 ✏️

Researchers used miniature solar-powered transmitters to track a male Rufous hummingbird from Alabama to Alaska, recording a 4,055-mile journey in 38 days—the longest hummingbird migration documented to date. They tagged the bird in Lillian, Alabama, on March 27, 2025, and it reached Juneau on May 3. The team fitted 11 hummingbirds with the devices in coastal Alabama and Florida in spring 2025 to track their movements across North America. The study authors said Rufous and ruby-throated hummingbird populations have recently declined; further research is needed to assess any long-term effects of wearing the transmitters.

items.title: [skyandtelescope.org] ESA's Euclid telescope finds record quasar beyond its survey reach
items.content_html: The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope identified a quasar candidate in its wide-area survey data, beyond the distance the mission was designed to map; ground- and space-based observatories then confirmed it. European Southern Observatory astronomer Julien Wolf led the discovery. The object, J1504+6252, was seen as it existed about 630 million years after the Big Bang. Follow-up observations with the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes, among other observatories, established its record distance. Euclid launched in 2023 to survey galaxies and help investigate dark matter and dark energy; the team published its findings in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

items.title: [earthsky.org] Simulations suggest hidden planet up to twice Earth's mass beyond Neptune
items.content_html: Computer models suggest a hypothetical planet dubbed Planet X2, with 1.5 to twice Earth’s mass, could help explain unusual orbits among icy objects beyond Neptune; the simulations do not establish that the planet exists. A peer-reviewed study published Nov. 23 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society places the proposed planet on an elongated orbit averaging 350 to 500 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun, with its closest approach at about 200 AU. The models reproduce several observed groupings of distant objects, but lead author Patryk Sofia Lykawka said differences between simulations and observations remain. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s sky survey could help test the predictions. Researchers say Planet X2 might coexist with a larger planet proposed under the separate Planet Nine hypothesis, or neither planet may exist.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.content_html: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

items.title: [theregister.com] ESA revises BepiColombo maneuvers after Mercury insertion software fault
items.content_html: The European Space Agency (ESA) has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software fault cut short the joint European-Japanese mission’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. ESA says the revised sequence can correct the spacecraft’s trajectory without additional thruster burns, keeping the separation of its two science orbiters and the start of science operations on schedule. The fault involved attitude guidance and thruster control, and the spacecraft entered a protective safe mode when the burn stopped. The spacecraft reached a stable Mercury orbit; ESA and its partners continue to investigate the software problem. The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mio orbiter remain joined and are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with routine science operations planned for April 2027. The European orbiter is expected to reach its final orbit in March, while Mio will investigate Mercury’s magnetosphere.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🔧 🪶 🌲 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Chile's Rubin Observatory survey could test hidden planet theory
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Chile’s Vera C. Rubin Observatory is conducting a decade-long survey that could help astronomers test whether distant icy bodies follow orbital patterns predicted for a hypothetical planet beyond Neptune. Its expanding catalogue will provide more objects to compare, but detecting the planet itself would be much harder because it would appear extremely faint. An international team led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka, a researcher at Japan’s Kindai University, used simulations of 4.5 billion years of Solar System evolution to propose Planet X2 as a possible explanation for some distant objects’ unusual orbits. Astronomers have not observed the planet, and the model does not match every feature of the known objects’ orbital distribution.

items.title: [physicsworld.com] Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions
items.content_html: Researchers propose that supercritical water in magma could explain how volcanic deposits formed more than 6,000 meters down the Mariana Trench wall, building on the discovery of unusually deep pyroclastic rocks. At those pressures, water behaves neither like an ordinary liquid nor a gas and expands far less than steam. The team says this may have enabled magma to fragment without the force of a land eruption. The mechanism remains uncertain: researchers have not found the vents or directly observed an eruption. Rock samples contain “double breccia,” suggesting two closely spaced episodes of fracturing — one possibly linked to supercritical fluid and another to its conversion to steam at the seafloor. The team plans further analysis of the volcanic material and aims to explore farther along the plate boundary. Jason/Medea cannot descend below 6,500 meters, short of the Challenger Deep floor at about 11,000 meters.

items.title: [science.nasa.gov] Webb finds evidence star’s layers may have merged before Cassiopeia A supernova
items.content_html: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has mapped dust in the Cassiopeia A supernova remnant, finding evidence that layers inside the original star merged shortly before it exploded—possibly in the final hours before core collapse. Webb’s observations indicate that signs of the merger occur across much of the remnant. The telescope detected silica-rich dust in one region and carbon-rich dust in another.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
items.content_html: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Voyager 1 reaches record distance of one light-day from Earth
items.content_html: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026, the farthest any human-made object has traveled. At about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers), a radio signal now takes 24 hours to travel one way between Earth and the probe. Voyager 1 continues to measure interstellar space, but its dwindling plutonium-powered electricity supply is forcing engineers to shut down equipment to conserve power. Its power output drops by about 4 watts a year, and the spacecraft could run out of power and go silent by 2036. A recent communications problem has also left engineers without science data to diagnose an onboard fault.

items.title: [phys.org] Deep-sea robot finds deepest volcanic deposits near Challenger Deep
items.content_html: The remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea has found what researchers describe as the deepest documented underwater pyroclastic deposits, on the Mariana Trench wall about 6,000 meters below sea level. The rocks provide evidence of volcanic flows in the trench’s western forearc, where geologists expected little volcanic activity because the mantle is generally not hot enough to melt. The findings were published Nov. 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science. The team’s observations support the idea that the Pacific Plate bends steeply as it sinks beneath the Mariana plate. That could help explain Challenger Deep’s depth and bring magma-generating processes closer to the trench. But researchers have not identified the eruption sites or established how eruptions could produce these deposits under immense water pressure. They say further sampling and radiometric dating are needed. Jason/Medea cannot reach the seafloor below 6,500 meters, while Challenger Deep extends to about 11,000 meters.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.content_html: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.content_html: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.
